lessons.title: Threads and `join`
lessons.book_section: 16.1 Using Threads to Run Code Simultaneously
lessons.objective_md: Start threads with `thread::spawn`, wait for them with `join`, and get their results back.

screens.heading: Doing two things at once
screens.text_md:
A **thread** is a separate line of execution inside your program. `thread::spawn` takes a closure and runs it on a new thread, while `main` carries on. The two print in an order the operating system decides, and it can change from one run to the next.

`spawn` returns a **`JoinHandle`**. `join()` waits for the thread to finish; without it, the program would end when `main` ends, possibly before the spawned thread had printed everything.

coming_from.c: Like `std::thread` and `join()`: an OS thread. Rust adds compile-time checks against data races.
coming_from.go: A thread is heavier than a goroutine: one OS thread each. Use a pool (P16-17) rather than thousands of threads.
coming_from.java: Like `new Thread(…).start()` and `join()`, or `Task.Run`. Rust uses one OS thread per `spawn`.
coming_from.js: JavaScript runs your code on one thread (workers aside). Rust threads share the process's memory and run at the same time, which is why the compiler checks what they touch.
coming_from.python: Like `threading.Thread(target=…).start()` and `.join()`, but Rust threads run truly in parallel: there's no global interpreter lock.

screens.heading: Threads can return values
screens.text_md: The closure's return value comes back through `join`, wrapped in a `Result`: `Ok(value)` if the thread finished normally, `Err` if it panicked. Returning results this way needs no shared state at all.

options.text_md: Waits for the thread to finish and returns its result.

explanations.text_md: Correct. It blocks until the thread is done, returning `Ok(value)` or `Err` if it panicked.
Not quite. The thread starts as soon as `spawn` is called.
Not quite. Rust has no way to kill a thread from outside.
Not quite. The thread runs separately; `join` only waits for it.

screens.heading: Where you join matters
screens.text_md:
Start all the threads first, then join them: they run at the same time. Joining each one right after starting it would make the program wait for each before starting the next, losing the parallelism.

Joining in the order the handles were made also fixes the order of the results, however the threads happen to finish.

screens.heading: A panicking thread
screens.text_md: A panic in a spawned thread ends that thread only. `join` reports it as an `Err`, and the main thread decides what to do. (The panic message itself still appears on standard error.)

panels.text:

question.prompt_md: If `main` returns without joining a spawned thread, that thread keeps running after the program ends.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. When `main` returns, the whole process ends, and every other thread is stopped wherever it was.
Correct. That's why you `join` threads whose work must finish.

screens.heading: Thread order is not program order
Sleeping is not synchronising
screens.text_md: `thread::sleep` pauses the current thread for at least a given time. It's useful in demonstrations to make interleaving visible, but it never *guarantees* an order: a slow machine can still run things differently. To wait for a thread, `join` it; later lessons add channels and locks.

lessons.book_section: 16.1 Using Threads to Run Code Simultaneously (`move` closures); `std::thread::scope`
lessons.objective_md: Give a thread ownership of its data with `move`, or borrow data safely with `thread::scope`.

screens.heading: A thread can't borrow a local
screens.text_md: The closure only reads `v`, so it would borrow it. But `thread::spawn` requires a closure that owns everything it uses (`'static`), because the new thread may outlive the function that started it (**E0373**).
screens.diagnostic:
error[E0373]: closure may outlive the current function, but it borrows `v`, which is owned by the current function
 --> src/main.rs:5:32
  |
5 |     let handle = thread::spawn(|| {
  |                                ^^ may outlive borrowed value `v`
6 |         println!("Here's a vector: {v:?}");
  |                                     - `v` is borrowed here
  |
help: to force the closure to take ownership of `v` (and any other referenced variables), use the `move` keyword
  |
5 |     let handle = thread::spawn(move || {
  |                                ++++

annotations.note_md: line 5: the compiler can't tell how long the thread will run; it might still be using `v` after `main` has dropped it.

screens.heading: `move` gives the thread ownership
screens.text_md: `move` makes the closure take ownership of `v`, so the thread owns the vector and can use it as long as it likes. `main` can't use `v` after this point: the ownership rules apply across threads too, which is exactly what stops two threads from touching the same data unsafely.

coming_from.c: Like capturing by move (`[v = std::move(v)]`) in a lambda passed to `std::thread`, but the compiler rejects the dangling-reference version.
coming_from.go: Like passing a value into a goroutine's function arguments, except the compiler then stops the caller using it.
coming_from.java: Java lambdas capture effectively-final variables by reference to shared objects. `move` transfers ownership instead, so only the thread can use the data.
coming_from.js: Like transferring a buffer to a Web Worker: after the move, the original side can't use it.
coming_from.python: Python threads can read any variable at any time. Rust makes you choose: hand the data to the thread (`move`), or share it with tools that make sharing safe.

question.prompt_md: Why does `thread::spawn` usually need a `move` closure?

options.text_md: The thread may outlive the variables of the function that started it, so it must own what it uses.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Owning the data means it can't be freed while the thread still uses it.
Not quite. `move` is about ownership, not speed.
Not quite. Any closure can return a value.
Not quite. It moves values; only `Copy` types end up copied.

screens.heading: Using a value after moving it
screens.text_md: This is the race the Book describes: `main` freeing data a thread is still reading. Ownership rules it out at compile time.

annotations.note_md: line 8: dropping it from `main` while the thread uses it would be a bug; the compiler refuses (**E0382**).

screens.heading: Borrowing with `thread::scope`
screens.text_md: `thread::scope` creates a scope in which you spawn threads with `s.spawn`. Every thread started in the scope is joined before `scope` returns, so the threads can't outlive anything they borrow. That makes plain borrowing safe: here two threads read halves of `v`, and `main` still owns it afterwards.

question.prompt_md: Threads spawned with `s.spawn` inside `thread::scope` can borrow local variables of the enclosing function without `move`.

explanations.text_md: Correct. The scope joins them all before it returns, so the borrows can't dangle.
Not quite. That guarantee is exactly what scoped threads add over `thread::spawn`.

screens.heading: `move` or scope?
screens.text_md:
Use **`move` with `thread::spawn`** when the thread should own its data and may run independently, for example a background worker that lives as long as the program.

Use **`thread::scope`** when you want to split work over data you already have, and wait for all of it before carrying on: the threads borrow, nothing is copied, and the joining is automatic.

Inside a scope you can still write `move` closures, to give each thread its own copy of something small like an index.

screens.heading: Moving small values into scoped threads
screens.text_md: Each closure needs its own `i`, so it's a `move` closure: `i` (a `usize`) and `words` (an array of `&str`, which is `Copy`) are copied in. The scope still makes sure no thread outlives the data.

question.general_md: `move` transfers `name` into the closure. The program prints `hi Ferris`.

wrong_answers.why_md: closures aren't borrowed with `&` here, and borrowing is what's rejected.

After `move`, the original variable can't be used (E0382); ownership prevents sharing by accident.
`thread::scope` joins all its threads before returning, so they may borrow local data.
`move` closures in a scope give each thread its own copy of small values.

lessons.title: Channels
lessons.book_section: 16.2 Using Message Passing to Transfer Data Between Threads
lessons.objective_md: Send values between threads through a channel, from one or several producers.

screens.heading: A channel
screens.text_md:
A **channel** has two halves: a **transmitter** (`tx`) that sends and a **receiver** (`rx`) that receives. `mpsc` stands for *multiple producer, single consumer*: many senders, one receiver.

`send` returns `Err` if the receiver is gone; `recv` waits until a value arrives, and returns `Err` once every sender is gone and no value is left.

coming_from.c: Like a thread-safe queue you'd build from a mutex and a condition variable, provided ready-made.
coming_from.go: Very close to Go channels: "share memory by communicating". `mpsc` channels are unbounded and have one receiver.
coming_from.java: Like a `BlockingQueue` or `Channel<T>`: producers put, a consumer takes.
coming_from.js: Like `postMessage` between workers, but values are moved, not copied.
coming_from.python: Like `queue.Queue` between threads: `put` and `get`. A Rust channel also moves ownership of what you send.

screens.heading: Sending moves the value
screens.text_md: Sending a value transfers ownership to whoever receives it. That's how channels avoid races: a value is only ever in one thread's hands.

annotations.note_md: line 8: `send` takes ownership; the receiving thread owns the `String` now.
line 9: using it here could race with the receiver changing or dropping it.

question.prompt_md: What does `rx.recv()` do when no message has arrived yet?

options.text_md: It waits until one arrives (or every sender is gone).
It returns the last message again.

explanations.text_md: Correct. `recv` blocks; `try_recv` is the version that doesn't wait.
Not quite. That's closer to `try_recv`, which returns an `Err` when nothing is waiting.
Not quite. Waiting is normal.
Not quite. Each message is received once.

screens.heading: Receiving until the senders are gone
screens.text_md: The receiver is an iterator: `for received in rx` receives each message in turn, and the loop ends when the channel closes, which happens when every sender has been dropped. Here the only sender lives in the thread, so the loop ends when the thread finishes.

screens.heading: Several producers
screens.text_md:
`tx.clone()` makes another sender for the same channel, one per producing thread. Messages from different threads arrive in whatever order the threads run, so here each one carries a number, and sorting puts them in a fixed order.

Both senders moved into threads, so the receiver's iteration ends once both threads are done.

question.prompt_md: Messages from two producer threads always arrive in the order the threads were started.

explanations.text_md: Not quite. The threads run independently; whichever sends first is received first.
Correct. Tag messages (with an index, say) when the order matters.

screens.heading: The receiver that waits forever
screens.text_md:
`for msg in rx` ends only when **every** sender is dropped. A common mistake is to clone `tx` for each worker and keep the original in the main thread: the workers finish, but the original sender still exists, so the loop waits forever and the program hangs.

The fix is one line: `drop(tx);` after starting the workers, before receiving. Then the channel closes when the last worker's sender goes.

screens.heading: Results in a fixed order
screens.text_md: One producer per item, each with its own sender clone; the original is dropped; results carry the item's index and are sorted back. This pattern gives the same answer however the threads are scheduled.

Sending transfers ownership, so no two threads use a value at once.
The receiver is an iterator that ends when every sender is dropped; `drop` the original sender after cloning it for workers.

lessons.title: `Mutex<T>`
lessons.objective_md: Protect shared data with a `Mutex<T>`, and keep each lock short.

screens.heading: One thread at a time
screens.text_md:
A **mutex** (mutual exclusion) lets only one thread at a time reach the data it guards. `Mutex::new(5)` puts the 5 inside; the only way in is `lock()`, which waits until no one else holds the lock and returns a **`MutexGuard`**.

The guard is a smart pointer: it derefs to the data (`*num = 6`), and when it's dropped, at the end of the block here, the lock is released automatically.

coming_from.c: Like `std::mutex` with `std::lock_guard`, but the mutex owns the data, so forgetting to lock doesn't compile.
coming_from.go: Like `sync.Mutex`, but the data is inside it and unlocking is automatic when the guard is dropped (no `defer mu.Unlock()`).
coming_from.java: Like a `synchronized` block or `lock` statement, with the protected data inside the lock object and the unlock tied to scope.
coming_from.js: Plain JavaScript has no shared-memory threads; with `SharedArrayBuffer` you'd use `Atomics`. Rust's `Mutex` guards whole values.
coming_from.python: Like `threading.Lock` used as `with lock:`, except the data lives *inside* the mutex, so you can't reach it without locking.

screens.heading: Locks in several threads
screens.text_md: Ten scoped threads each add 1 under the lock. Each `+=` happens while that thread alone holds the guard, so no update is lost, and the result is always 10. (`thread::scope` lets the threads borrow `counter`; L16.5 shares it with `thread::spawn` instead.)

options.text_md: When the `MutexGuard` returned by `lock()` is dropped.

explanations.text_md: Correct. Dropping the guard (usually at the end of its scope) unlocks the mutex.
Not quite. There's no `unlock` method; the guard's `Drop` does it.
Not quite. The guard is dropped long before, usually.
Not quite. Locks don't expire.

screens.heading: Check and change under one lock
screens.text_md: Five buyers, three items. Each thread checks and decrements under the **same** guard. If a thread checked, released the lock, then locked again to decrement, two threads could both see `1` and sell the last item twice. Whatever must stay true (here: never sell what isn't there) has to be protected by one critical section.

screens.heading: Deadlocks

question.prompt_md: Calling `m.lock()` twice in the same thread, while the first guard is still alive, waits forever (or panics).

explanations.text_md: Correct. The second call waits for the first guard, which can't be dropped while the thread waits. The standard library may detect it and panic, but you can't rely on that.
Not quite. A `Mutex` isn't re-entrant.

screens.heading: Poisoning
screens.text_md: If a thread panics while holding a guard, the mutex is **poisoned**: the data might be half-changed, so later `lock()` calls return `Err`. Usually that's a bug, and `expect` turns it into a panic. When you know how to check or repair the data, `into_inner()` on the error still gives you the guard (P16-11).

screens.heading: `Mutex` and `RefCell`
screens.text_md:
`Mutex<T>` gives interior mutability like `RefCell<T>`: you change data through a shared reference, and the rules are enforced while the program runs. The differences:

| | `RefCell<T>` | `Mutex<T>` |
|---|---|---|
| Threads | one | many |
| A conflicting access | panics | waits for the lock |
| Access | `borrow` / `borrow_mut` | `lock` |

question.general_md: `lock()` returns the guard (in a `Result`); the program prints `15`.

summary: `Mutex<T>` holds data that only one thread at a time can reach, through `lock()`.
`lock()` returns a `MutexGuard` that derefs to the data and unlocks when dropped.
Keep every check and change that must stay consistent inside one guard; keep guards short.
Deadlocks stop the program silently; a panic while holding a lock poisons the mutex.

screens.heading: A mutex can only move once
screens.text_md: With `thread::spawn`, each thread needs to *own* the mutex, but a value has one owner. Several owners is what `Rc` gave in Chapter 15, so we need that, made safe for threads.

screens.heading: Lock less, work more
screens.text_md: Each thread does its work on its own data first (summing its chunk), and locks the shared total only once, for the final `+=`. Threads that hold a lock make others wait, so the less time spent holding it, the more work runs in parallel.

screens.heading: `Arc` or scoped threads?
screens.text_md:
Both let several threads use one value:

- **`thread::scope`** lets threads *borrow* data the current function owns, and joins them before it returns. Nothing is counted or shared; there's no `Arc` at all.

Prefer scoped threads for "split this work and wait"; use `Arc` when threads run independently.

screens.heading: `Arc<Mutex<T>>` and `Rc<RefCell<T>>`

| `Rc<RefCell<T>>` | `Arc<Mutex<T>>` |

lessons.title: `Send` and `Sync`
lessons.book_section: 16.4 Extensible Concurrency with the `Send` and `Sync` Traits
lessons.objective_md: Know what `Send` and `Sync` mean and how they let the compiler stop data races.

screens.heading: Two marker traits
screens.text_md:
Rust's thread safety rests on two traits that have no methods; they only mark what a type allows:

- **`Send`**: a value of this type can be **moved** to another thread.
- **`Sync`**: a value of this type can be **shared** between threads, that is, `&T` can be used from several threads at once.

`thread::spawn` requires its closure to be `Send`, so everything it captures must be `Send`. Sharing a reference across threads requires the type to be `Sync`.

coming_from.c: Nothing in C++ marks types as thread-safe; data races are undefined behaviour. In Rust they're compile errors.
coming_from.go: Go's race detector finds races while tests run; Rust's `Send` and `Sync` reject them before the program runs.
coming_from.java: There's no compile-time equivalent; thread-safety is up to documentation and discipline. Rust checks it.
coming_from.js: Like the structured-clone rules for what can be posted to a worker, but checked by the compiler for every type.
coming_from.python: Python has no such checks; thread-safety is documented, not enforced. Rust's compiler refuses code that would race.

screens.heading: Which types have them
screens.text_md:
Almost every type is both. The compiler works it out from the fields: a struct is `Send` if all its fields are, and likewise for `Sync`. The exceptions are types that would allow a race:

- `Rc<T>` is neither: its count isn't atomic.
- `RefCell<T>` is `Send` but not `Sync`: one thread may own it, but its borrow tracking isn't safe to share.
- `Mutex<T>` and `Arc<T>` (of `Send`/`Sync` contents) are both: they're built to be shared.

Functions with a bound, like `is_send`, compile only for types that have the trait, a handy check.

explanations.text_md: Correct. `T: Sync` means `&T` is safe to share.
Not quite. That's `Send`.
Not quite. Being `Sync` doesn't add locking; `Mutex` is `Sync` because it locks.
Not quite. `Mutex<T>` is `Sync` and allows changes.

screens.text_md: Two threads could run `borrow_mut` at exactly the same moment and both succeed, because `RefCell`'s check isn't atomic. Use a `Mutex<i32>` instead and it compiles.

screens.heading: Moving a `RefCell` is fine
screens.text_md: Moving the cell gives the new thread sole ownership; no other thread can reach it, so there's nothing to race with. `RefCell` is `Send`, so this compiles. The distinction is exactly the one between the two traits: owning in one thread at a time (`Send`) versus using from several at once (`Sync`).

explanations.text_md: Not quite. `Send` and `Sync` are implemented automatically when all fields have them.

problems.description_md: Write `squares(n)`, which starts `n` threads, the `i`-th computing `i * i` for `i` from 0 to `n - 1`, and returns their results in that order. Start **all** the threads first, keeping their handles in a `Vec`, and only then join them one by one. (Joining each thread right after starting it would run them one at a time.)
hints: `let handles: Vec<_> = (0..n).map(|i| thread::spawn(move || i as u64 * i as u64)).collect();`
Then `handles.into_iter().map(|h| h.join().expect("worker panicked")).collect()`.
Joining in handle order gives results in thread order, however the threads finish.
problems.solution_approach_md: The first iterator chain starts every thread before anything is joined, so they run at the same time. Joining the handles in the order they were made returns the results in that order: if a later thread finishes first, its result simply waits until its turn.
problems.idiomatic_md: The order threads *finish* is up to the operating system; the order you *join* them is up to you. Collect results by join order (or by a tag) to make output deterministic.

Each thread counts its chunk in a **local** array first and then adds that array to the shared `Arc<Mutex<[u32; 4]>>` under **one** lock, so each thread locks once instead of once per value.
hints: `for chunk in values.chunks(8) { let owned = chunk.to_vec(); let bins = Arc::clone(&bins); … }` — the thread needs its own copy of the chunk.
In the thread: `let mut local = [0u32; 4]; for v in owned { local[(v % 4) as usize] += 1; }`
Then `let mut shared = bins.lock().expect("…"); for i in 0..4 { shared[i] += local[i]; }`
problems.solution_approach_md: Counting locally needs no lock at all; only the merge touches shared state, once per thread. After every thread is joined, the shared array holds the counts of all chunks.
problems.idiomatic_md: Holding a lock for as short a time and as few times as possible is how parallel code stays fast: threads waiting on a lock are threads doing nothing.

problems.title: Move a cell without sharing it
problems.description_md:
`Send` means a value may be **moved** to another thread; `Sync` means it may be **shared** (`&T` used from several threads). `RefCell<T>` is `Send` but not `Sync`: one thread may own it, but two may not share it.

1. Write `is_send<T: Send>(_: &T) -> bool` and `is_sync<T: Sync>(_: &T) -> bool`, each simply returning `true`: they compile only for types that have the trait.
2. Write `move_cell(value)`, which puts `value` in a `RefCell`, moves the cell into a new thread that adds 1 (saturating) through `borrow_mut`, and returns the final value with `into_inner`.
hints: Add the bounds: `pub fn is_send<T: Send>(_: &T) -> bool { true }`.
`let cell = RefCell::new(value); thread::spawn(move || { … cell.into_inner() })`
The thread owns the cell, so `borrow_mut` inside it is fine.
problems.solution_approach_md: The bound does the checking: calling `is_send` with a non-`Send` type is a compile error, so a function body of `true` is honest. Moving the `RefCell` gives the thread sole ownership, which `Send` allows; it changes the value and returns it.
problems.idiomatic_md: You almost never implement `Send` or `Sync` yourself: the compiler derives them from the fields. Implementing them by hand requires `unsafe` and is for types like `Mutex` that build the safety themselves.

- Required: the compiler probe `let c = std::cell::RefCell::new(1); std::thread::scope(|s| { s.spawn(|| *c.borrow_mut() += 1); s.spawn(|| *c.borrow_mut() += 1); });` is rejected with `E0277`.

problems.title: Restore order from a worker pool
problems.description_md:
Build a small **worker pool**. `reverse_all(texts, workers)` reverses every text (by `char`, so `"abc"` becomes `"cba"`) using a fixed number of threads:

1. Put the jobs, `(index, text)` pairs, in a queue shared by the workers: an `Arc<Mutex<VecDeque<(usize, String)>>>`.
2. Start `workers` threads (at least 1, at most 8, and never more than there are texts). Each loops: lock the queue, take the front job, **release the lock**, reverse the text, and send `(index, reversed)` through a channel. When the queue is empty, it stops.
3. Collect the results, join the workers, and return the reversed texts in input order.
problems.constraints_md: - Up to 1,000 texts; any `workers` value (clamped as described). No `unwrap()`.
hints: `let count = workers.clamp(1, 8).min(texts.len());` — with no texts, start no workers.
Take a job so the guard is dropped at once: `let job = queue.lock().expect("…").pop_front();` then `match job { Some((i, t)) => …, None => break }`.
Drop the original sender after starting the workers, collect `(usize, String)` pairs from the receiver, sort by index.
problems.solution_approach_md: Each worker holds the queue's lock only while taking a job, so reversing and sending happen without blocking the others. Results come back tagged with their index, in whatever order the workers finish; sorting by index restores the input order. Dropping the original sender lets the receiver's iteration end when the last worker exits.
problems.idiomatic_md: This is the shape of the thread pool in Chapter 21: a shared job queue, a fixed set of workers, and a way to know when they're done.

problems.title: Reserve stock concurrently
problems.description_md:
A shop has `stock` units and receives `requests` orders for one unit each. Write `reserve(stock, requests, workers)`, which handles the orders with a pool of worker threads sharing one `Arc<Mutex<Shop>>`:

```rust
pub struct Shop {
    pub stock: u32,
    pub handled: usize,
    pub sold: usize,
}
```

Each worker loops: under **one** lock, if every order has been handled (`handled == requests`) it stops; otherwise it handles one order (`handled += 1`) and, if stock is left, sells a unit (`stock -= 1; sold += 1`). Use `workers.clamp(1, 8)` threads, but none when there are no requests. Return the final `(stock, sold)`.

Claiming an order and selling for it in one critical section is what guarantees that no order is handled twice and no unit is sold twice.
hints: `let shop = Arc::new(Mutex::new(Shop { stock, handled: 0, sold: 0 }));`
In each worker: `loop { let mut s = shop.lock().expect("…"); if s.handled == requests { break; } s.handled += 1; if s.stock > 0 { s.stock -= 1; s.sold += 1; } }`
After joining: `let s = shop.lock().expect("…"); (s.stock, s.sold)`.
problems.solution_approach_md: The shared `Shop` records how many orders are handled as well as the stock, so workers agree on when to stop. Everything one order does happens under one guard, so orders and units can't be double-counted however the threads interleave. The result is the same on every run: `sold = min(stock, requests)`.
problems.idiomatic_md: Keeping all related counters behind one lock is simpler and safer than several locks, which can be taken in inconsistent orders and deadlock.
problems.random_md: For each case draw `stock = pick(50)`, `requests = pick(50)` and `workers = pick(10)`. Call `crate::reserve`. Use the common generator, seed `0x10000012`, exactly 300 cases.

problems.title: Merge parallel sorted runs
problems.description_md:
Write `parallel_sorted(values, parts)`, which sorts a copy of `values` using several threads:

1. Split the slice into `parts.clamp(1, 8)` chunks (never more chunks than values), of length `len.div_ceil(count)` except perhaps the last.
2. In a `thread::scope`, give each chunk to a thread that copies it into a `Vec` and sorts it.
3. Join the threads in chunk order and **merge** their sorted runs into one sorted vector, two at a time. Don't sort the combined result again.

The input slice is not changed, and every value is kept, duplicates included.
hints: `merge`: two indexes; push the smaller front item (the left one on ties), then append whatever is left of either side.
`let size = values.len().div_ceil(count);` and `values.chunks(size)`; return early for an empty slice.
In the scope: spawn one sorting thread per chunk, then `let mut result = Vec::new(); for h in handles { result = merge(&result, &h.join().expect("…")); }`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Each thread sorts its own chunk in parallel, borrowing the input through the scope. The coordinator merges runs as it joins them: merging two sorted runs walks both from the front, always taking the smaller item, so the result is sorted in one pass without re-sorting.
problems.idiomatic_md: This is a parallel merge sort with one level of splitting. Real code would reach for a crate like `rayon`; the scope-and-merge pattern is what it does underneath.

problems.title: Dispatch a shared callback safely
problems.description_md:
Write `parallel_map(input, workers, f)`, which applies `f` to every input value on a pool of threads and returns the results in input order. Only the signature's bounds are given: `F: Fn(u32) -> u64 + Send + Sync + 'static`. Several threads call the **same** `f`, so it's shared with an `Arc<F>`; that's why it must be `Sync` (shared between threads), `Send` (the `Arc` moves into threads) and `'static` (the threads may outlive the call's borrows).

Use `workers.clamp(1, 8)` threads (none for empty input), a shared job queue and a result channel as in P16-17. Call `f` **exactly once per item**, and never while holding the queue lock.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::parallel_map(vec![1, 2, 3], 2, |x| x as u64 * 10)
Expected:   vec![10, 20, 30]
```
hints: `let f = Arc::new(f);` and give each worker `Arc::clone(&f)`.
Take a job and drop the guard before calling: `let job = queue.lock().expect("…").pop_front();`.
Send `(index, f(value))`, then sort the collected pairs by index.
problems.solution_approach_md: The callback is shared, not copied: `Arc<F>` gives every worker a handle to the one closure, and the bounds let the compiler check that doing so is thread-safe. Jobs are taken under the queue lock and processed outside it, so a slow callback doesn't block the other workers. Tagged results are sorted back into input order.
problems.idiomatic_md: `Fn` doesn't mean "no side effects": a callback can count calls through an `Arc<Mutex<…>>` or an atomic. The tests use that to check it's called exactly once per item.

problems.title: Parallel word counter
problems.comes_after: All chapter lessons and one Medium Accepted
problems.description_md:
Count words in many texts with a pool of threads, in the library package `wordcount`. A word is what `split_whitespace` finds, compared exactly: no case folding, no punctuation stripping.

**Part 1 · Counting one text**

`count_one(text)` returns every distinct word of `text` with how many times it appears, as `(word, count)` pairs sorted by word. No threads yet.

**Part 2 · A pool of counters**

`count_all(texts, workers)` counts all the texts together. Use `workers.clamp(1, 8)` threads, never more than there are texts (none for no texts). The texts go in a shared queue (`Arc<Mutex<VecDeque<String>>>`); each worker repeatedly takes one text (releasing the lock at once), counts it into its **own** `HashMap<String, u64>`, and when the queue is empty sends that map through a channel. The caller merges the maps and returns the pairs sorted by word.

**Part 3 · The most common words**

`top(texts, workers, n)` returns the first `n` pairs of `count_all`'s result reordered by count, highest first, with equal counts by word.

**Part 4 · The same answer every time**

Nothing new to write: these rows run the pool many times, with many texts and many workers, and expect identical results.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: crate::count_all(vec![String::from("a b a"), String::from("b c")], 2)
Expected:   vec![("a".to_string(), 2), ("b".to_string(), 2), ("c".to_string(), 1)]
```
problems.constraints_md: - Up to 1,000 texts, 1 MB in total. No `unwrap()`.
hints: A helper `fn add_words(map: &mut HashMap<String, u64>, text: &str)` with `*map.entry(word.to_string()).or_insert(0) += 1;` serves both `count_one` and the workers.
Each worker: `let mut local = HashMap::new(); loop { let job = queue.lock().expect("…").pop_front(); match job { Some(t) => add_words(&mut local, &t), None => break } } tx.send(local)…`
Merge with `for map in rx { for (w, c) in map { *total.entry(w).or_insert(0) += c; } }`, then collect and sort.
problems.solution_approach_md: Every count happens in a worker's own map, so no lock is needed while counting; the queue's lock is held only to take a job. Each worker sends one map when it's done, and the caller merges them. A `HashMap` has no order, so sorting the merged pairs (by word, or by count then word in `top`) makes the result the same on every run.
problems.idiomatic_md: "Map then reduce": independent local work followed by one merge is the easiest kind of parallelism to get right, because the threads never touch shared data while working.

The case's result is `(count_all(texts, workers), top(texts, workers, k))`. Use the course generator, seed `0x10010000`, exactly 300 cases.

problems.title: Searching in parallel
problems.description_md:
The starter is the LM15 workspace with a new module, `core/src/concurrent.rs` (`pub mod concurrent;` is already in `core/src/lib.rs`). Use threads to serve many searches and to load many catalogs at once. The rest of the library is unchanged.

**Part 1 · Can the library be shared?**

`library_is_shareable()` returns `true` and compiles only if `Library` is `Send` and `Sync`: call a helper `fn assert_shareable<T: Send + Sync>() {}` with `Library`. (It is: all its fields are plain owned data.)

**Part 2 · Many searches at once**

`search_many(library, queries, workers)` runs `library.find(query)` for every query and returns, for each query in input order, the ids of the books it finds. Split the queries into `workers.clamp(1, 8)` chunks (never more chunks than queries) and search each chunk in a thread of a `thread::scope`, borrowing the library. Join the threads in chunk order and concatenate their results.

**Part 3 · Loading catalogs in parallel**

`load_many(catalogs)` loads every catalog text with `cli::load_catalog`, each in its own `thread::spawn`ed thread (the texts are moved in), and returns for each catalog in input order either `Ok(number of books)` or the catalog's error. Each thread sends `(index, result)` through a channel; sort by index.
problems.examples_md:
```text
Expression: { let lib = crate::cli::load_catalog("Dune|Frank Herbert|1965\nEmma|Jane Austen|1815\n").expect("valid"); crate::concurrent::search_many(&lib, vec![String::from("emma"), String::from("x")], 2) }
Expected:   vec![vec![2], vec![]]
```
problems.constraints_md: - Up to 1,000 queries and 100 catalogs. No `unwrap()`, no `unsafe`.
hints: `fn assert_shareable<T: Send + Sync>() {}` then `assert_shareable::<Library>(); true`.

`let size = queries.len().div_ceil(count);` and in the scope `queries.chunks(size).map(|chunk| s.spawn(move || chunk.iter().map(|q| library.find(q).iter().map(|b| b.id).collect()).collect::<Vec<Vec<u32>>>()))`.
`load_many`: `for (i, text) in catalogs.into_iter().enumerate() { let tx = tx.clone(); thread::spawn(move || tx.send((i, load_catalog(&text).map(|l| l.find("").len()))) … }`.
problems.solution_approach_md: Because `Library` is `Sync`, scoped threads can share `&Library` and search it at the same time; the scope guarantees the borrows end before `search_many` returns. Chunks are joined in order, so concatenating their results keeps the query order. Catalog loading needs no sharing at all: each thread owns its text and builds its own `Library`, and tagged results are sorted back into order.
problems.idiomatic_md: Read-only sharing needs no lock: `&T` across threads is safe exactly when `T: Sync`, which the compiler checks for you.
